speechtext: Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata) (Translation): In yesterday's Hansard at page 2777, the hon. Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) charged me with having raised the war cry in the course of the last election. Such tactics is like beating the air. speechtext: This is a bill providing for the grading of potatoes.
Radishes?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, that is left for my hon. friend from Weyburn (Mr. Young). The former statute provided for the grading of old potatoes only, not new. This bill removes that anomaly and provides for grading both old and new.

The purpose of the bill,
which on the face of it appears so simple, undoubtedly is to bring under the grading provisions those new potatoes that come into the country very early in the season. I would judge therefore that this bill is but a further indication of the protective measures of the present government. I think I have interpreted the bill correctly.

I was just wondering what new conditions had arisen which would make the grading of new potatoes advisable at this time. Some years ago it was thought that we were crowding this grading proposition as fast as the country would accept it. Probably the country will never accept this further advanced step, or it may be that there are new conditions which render the step advisable. I wonder what those conditions are. I must explain that I am not opposing the bill but I am curious to know what new circumstances have arisen which make it necessary.

I think we are discussing the wrong section. I may call the attention of hon. members to the fact that section 2 deals with the grading of new potatoes but section 1 has nothing whatever to do with that matter. As will be seen by the side note on the bill, section 1 deals merely with the marking of packages. Section 1, if passed, would do away with the marking of packages. The reason given for the repeal of the section is that this particular matter is provided for by section 3 (d) of the act. I have not the act before me at the present time because I did not anticipate the matter would come before the committee to-day. When we reach section 2, I should like to make some remarks concerning the grading of new potatoes.

Royal Canadian Mint

Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide for the establishment of the Royal Canadian Mint as a branch of the Department of Finance, and to make provision for the payment of salaries and for superannuation and retiring benefits of members of the staff of the Ottawa mint on the coming into force of the proposed legislation.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. MacDonald (Cape Breton) in the chair.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this resolution is for the purpose of introducing a bill which will provide for the transfer of the administration of the mint from the Royal Mint, London, to the Canadian government under the Department of Finance. Provision is made for the changes that are incidental in connection with such a transfer, such as superannuation, arrangement of salaries and so on. The matter has engaged the attention of the government for some time, and last fall I took it up with the Chancellor of the Exchequer in London. This legislation is the result. If it meets with the approval of the house, when the bill founded upon the resolution has been introduced and given second reading, in committee I shall be glad to give such particulars as members may require. No useful purpose would be served in taking up the time of the house to do so now in the light of the resolution, which does not furnish details.

Mr. Chairman, I agree
with the right hon. gentleman that any comment might be reserved until the bill is before the committee. Meanwhile I want to say that I endorse very strongly the principle of this legislation.
Mr. LaVERGNE: May I add, Mr. Chairman, that I think the purpose of this legislation is in accordance with the spirit of the constitution. Our coin should be minted in Canada, and should be bilingual according to the traditions of the British Empire and in consonance with the spirit of our constitution. Bilingual coinage is in circulation in South Africa, in Switzerland and in Belgium. I think our coins should be distinguished from those of the republic to our south, whose pennies and five-cent pieces particularly we are copying to a very great extent. Our coins should be bilingual, in accordance with our constitution.

Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Bennett thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 101, respecting the establishment of the Royal Canadian Mint.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act be amended to provide for the appointment of a comptroller of the treasury with duties, salary and tenure of office as prescribed, and to secure a more unified and adequate control over administration of the act and of financial receipts and expenditure.
Motion agreed to, and the house went into committee, Mr. LaVergne in the chair.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think it would best suit the convenience of the committee if we were to pass the resolution and give the bill founded upon it first reading. On the second reading I wovdd propose to give the house a short resume of just what is involved. Briefly, it contemplates the centralizing in the Department of Finance of the financial control of the business of the country.
I have a large amount of detail which I shall be glad to furnish the house either on the first or second reading, but to do it twice I think perhaps would be regarded as unnecessary. If it is thought desirable I might give it now, but my idea was to secure second reading of the bill and refer it to the committee on banking and commerce in order that they might discuss the details of the measure and determine whether or not adequate provision has been made for every contingency which might arise. It may amaze the committee to know that there has been substantially no change in the general accounting principles governing the conduct of business in Canada since 1878. The officials of the department have been giving much attention to the matter, and it is one about which I have rather a strqng opinion, which I shall be glad to give to the house when the second reading of the measure is being sought.
At the moment the statement contained in the resolution is a very general resume of what is involved. The comptroller of the treasury, and the control of the whole expenditure of all the departments of the public service in Canada-

Revenue and Audit Act

Will that comptroller
have new duties altogether, or will his duties be what are part of the duties of the Deputy Minister of Finance to-day?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That question could be properly answered by saying both. He will have some new duties, and he will not to any appreciable extent discharge the duties of the Deputy Minister of Finance. He will coordinate the accounting of all the departments under a central control, and provision is made in the bill founded upon the resolution for the position of the auditor general to be more clearly defined. Perhaps hon. gentlemen will recall that the auditor general at the moment is a statutory official, whose salary is provided by statute in part only, and in part in the estimates. This bill will render him entirely free from the estimates and provide for his salary to be a charge upon the consolidated revenue fund, which was thought to be very important fifty years ago but which, in recent times, has not been so regarded.
I can do one of two things; I am entirely in the hands of the committee. If the committee desires I will go into the matter in detail now or upon the second reading.
I think the second reading would be better.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I should think so, and perhaps it would be the more proper time, because then the principle of the measure is involved. With that understanding, I merely move the resolution.

I should like to ask a question now which it might not be possible to ask on the second reading. Will the new comptroller of the treasury be responsible to the government of the day as such or to parliament? The reason I ask the question is that in some of the provinces, as my right hon. friend knows, the comptroller general is only responsible to parliament and not to the government of the day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I thank my hon. friend for raising that point. The position of this official is not quite that of comptroller general. The Minister of Finance would be directly responsible to parliament, and the *comptroller general would be an official of that department for whom, of course, the minister must be entirely responsible. I quite appreciate the point to which the hon. gentleman refers; I think he will find it dealt with in a manner which will be satisfactory to the country.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Bennett thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 102 to amend the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. LaVergne in the chair.
Public Works-roads and bridges, $173,250.

When this item was
last under discussion I asked the minister for some information regarding the workmen employed by contractors in the interprovincial bridge between Hawkesbury and Grenville. Can the minister give an explanation now of the shortage in wages paid these men?

speakeroldname: Hon. H. A. STEWART (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
Since this item was under consideration on the former occasion I have investigated the matter and ascertained the facts to be as follows. Under the contract the contractor was bound to pay a fixed schedule of wages, but for a part of the time he did not fully comply with the contract in that respect. The matter was checked up by the Department of Labour in the regular course. They do this of their own motion from time to time, as we give them a list of the contracts. I am informed by that department that one of its representatives went to the work and interviewed the contractor and labourers, and that an arrangement was made which appears to have been satisfactory to all concerned at that time. The arrangement was that the contractor should continue the work during the winter months, at some greater expense to himself, thus furnishing employment which otherwise would not have been available, and that he should carry on that work although the funds were not available in that way also providing work. The Labour department seemed to be well satisfied with that arrangement and it has, I believe, been carried out. Since the last meeting of this committee, however, I have issued instructions to the deputy minister to get in touch with the Labour department and to have a representative go over the whole situation again with a view to seeing that the contract was complied with in respect to work remaining to be done. We reserve the right to decide whether full justice has been done in the matter.

Supply-Public Works
Am I to understand that the schedule which was included in the contract given to the contractor is not going to be fully observed?

No, quite the
contrary. Unless the Department of Labour and the Public Works department can be satisfied that labour has been fully compensated and taken care of, either directly, in the wage schedule, or in some other way, which provided work at a time when it would not otherwise have been available, then the matter will not be satisfactory to either department.
Surely the minister is not serious in that statement.

Yes; he is
very serious.

Well, I am surprised that he is. I have never heard of such a thing in my life. The specifications were prepared and included in the tenders which were called for this pubEc work, and every contractor who bid on the work had specifications before him and knew what wages were to be paid. And then some department of the government or some officer of the government makes a different arrangement. I have never heard of such a thing. You might just as well say that any department or officer of the government can change any specification after the contractor has received the contract. The minister shakes his head. What is the difference between wages and any other specification that might be in the contract? I have under my hand the Labour Gazette of October, 1930, in which the government advertises to the world the wages that were being paid on that job. I shall not read them all, but it provides for engineers, carpenters, masons and so on, down to labourers at forty-five cents an hour. After the contractor has bid, declaring that he will carry out the specifications, some department or the government itself cannot alter that in any way.
I can see this point in the minister's argument; there might be same extenuating circumstances as between the government and the contractors. The contractors might be requested to undertake and might carry out works at an untimely season. If that be true, the wages of the men ought not to be reduced in order to compensate the contractors. The government ought to compensate the contractors in respect of any extenuating circumstances. If the minister will just think the matter over, he will realize that the men's 
wages ought not to be reduced from those specified in the contract, in order that the contractor may be induced to proceed with the work at an unseasonable time. If any compensation is coming to the contractor, it should come from the government and not from the men. We have had cases of a similar character. Just before the Conservative government went out of power, I think it was in 1921, there was a case similar to this in Quebec where a contractor was called upon to build a dry dock, and owing to the war and the increase in wages some extra expense was involved. But the government took into consideration those extenuating circumstances and paid the contractor some additional money. Could, however, anyone imagine that a department or the government would reduce the wages of the men in order to compensate the contractor? The minister ought to take that into consideration.

The government did not ask the contractor to proceed with the work. He himself, after consultation with the labourers, with their full approval, largely for their benefit, and to compensate for the smaller amount which had been paid, agreed to continue the work and to give them employment at a time when it was not otherwise advisable. The government did not request, and knew nothing about it until after the arrangement had been made. This matter was adjusted through the Department of Labour, and as I say the matter is still under review with that department, with the deputy minister, with a view to seeing that labour is fully taken care of in respect of this contract.

If the government did not
consent to the carrying on of the work, the contractor went on without the government's knowledge. Was the work laid out by the engineers of the department before the contractor undertook to carry out the contract?

They did not
ask him to carry it out during the winter; he had the option of continuing or stopping.

The contractor had begun
the work before the winter season came on. It was up to him to continue or to stop it during the winter season.
It was up to the contractor.

It was no business of the
department to ask the men to accept lower wages.

Supply-Public Works
The government did not ask the contractor to proceed with the work.

Then they did not care
whether unemployment was relieved or not. If I am not mistaken, from information laid before the committee the last time this item was under discussion, the wages paid to the common labourer amounted to forty-five cents an hour. The contractor began the work by paying thirty-five cents; later on that was increased to forty cents and continued at that figure. If that be correct; if a contractor who tendered for and received a contract on the basis of forty-five cents an hour for labourers, is allowed to begin by paying thirty-five cents and later is forced to pay forty cents and is allowed to keep it there, he is making a profit of five cents an hour on every man he engages on that work. He calculated that it would cost him forty-five cents an hour for common labour and he has been allowed to engage common labourers and to keep them at work at forty cents an hour. There was no attempt on the part of the department, when the contractor was paying only forty cents an hour, to make him live up to the agreement of forty-five cents until the attention of the department was drawn to the matter and even then the rate was allowed to remain at forty cents. Does the minister mean to say that is the way to carry on a work of that character? The regulations distinctly state what shall be done; it is definitely set forth that the rate of pay for common labourers shall be forty-five cents an hour. The contractor undertakes to carry out that schedule; he tenders on that schedule; he knows exactly what the labour is going to cost him per hour. Yet the department allows him to continue paying forty cents an hour and to make five cents an hour profit on each labourer. If there are 100 men working the contractor makes a profit of $40 daily, and yet he is allowed to proceed and to take his profits out of the labouring men instead of taking his chances under his tender of making what profit he can by paying legitimate wages in regard to which he signed a contract and gave a bond. He put up a deposit; he gave a bond, but he is not carrying out that contract, and yet the minister allows him to continue.

The matter is not closed. It is still under review. The work is not completed and there is plenty of time to deal with the contractor and hold something in reserve.
22U0-1791
Will the minister deal with the contractor along those lines?

As I said before, the matter will be considered in all its aspects with the cooperation of the Department of Labour which is primarily responsible for the carrying out of that particular part of the contract. The matter will be disposed of fairly to the men. That is all I can say.

I do not think the minister is going far enough in saying that the matter will be considered. We have sufficient evidence now to show that the contractor never intended to live up to his contract with respect to the payment of wages. I was not aware of this until the ex-Postmaster General made his statement. The contractor commenced by jpaying thirty^five cents an hour notwithstanding the fact that his contract calls for forty-five cents. Apparently some officer of the Labour department checked him up and then he paid forty cents an hour. I can readily understand the difficulties in connection with fair wages oil any public contract. I have had sufficient experience to know that in practically every contract that is let there is a dispute between the contractor and the men. The men do not seem to feel they are getting enough, while the contractor says that if wages are any higher he will fail on the contract. to advantage at this season of the year; we have been paying the men forty-five cents an hour, but we are prepared to carry it on at a little disadvantage to ourselves provided that the matter can be adjusted by a lowering of wages, that would have been a different proposition. No sooner did he receive the contract than he cut the schedule down to thirty-five cents an hour and the department allowed that. But if the work was begun in October, in the river where this bridge crosses no ice forms earlier than December which would be of disadvantage to a contractor. All the advantage would be on his side to have his piers and abutments constructed to such an elevation as to be beyond the freshet level in the spring of the year. Everything was to the contractors's advantage that the men should work during the frosty season. Where is there any great disadvantage to a contractor doing construction work in the winter time with all the modern improvements and heating apparatus which they have? Some of the finest buildings in the Dominion of Canada were constructed in the winter when we have twenty-five to thirty degrees of frost. Contractors consider it an advantage, with modern appliances, to be able to carry on work of this sort to a certain point so that in the spring of the year they may press it forward. This is particularly true of bridge construction across rivers where there are heavy freshets in the spring of the year. We know last fall was one of the best seasons in the vicinity of Ottawa and up through Prescott county on account of the low level of the water. Under the conditions that obtained in this case, the advantage was all on the side of the contractor and not on that of the workmen, but he took advantage of the men because the department allowed him to pay them thirty-five cents instead of forty-five cents an hour. When later on he was checked up, he forced the men to accept forty cents an hour.

For some years, as the minister knows, I occupied the position of Deputy Minister of Labour. For a time also I was Minister of Labour. During that period the kind of thing that is reported in this instance was being suggested every now and then to the department by contractors. Over and over again the request was made that the department agree to allow the rates to be reduced on the understanding that upon agreement compensation would be made in other respects. The reply invariably made was that it would be unfair to other contractors who had tendered on the assumption that they would have to pay the scale that was fixed and was before them at the time they tendered. That is a strong position for the department to take, and I do not see how any contractor can complain if he had before him the schedule and made his tender on the basis of the rates set forth therein. Moreover, the schedule is there to protect labour against the sort of pressure contractors are able at times to exert. The minister's assurance is, I believe, sufficient to cause us to believe that he will be able to see that the contractor complies with the law.

I accept the suggestion of my right hon. friend. I am glad he has given me that information, but I want to say that neither the Department of Public Works nor the Department of Labour was approached with any view to consenting to a variation in conditions. As soon as a variation was found to exist, the Department of Labour undertook to have it adjusted and to do what they thought at the time was fair and reasonable, and they brought about what they believed to be a fair and satisfactory adjustment to all the labourers. That, however, does not appear to satisfy the committee, and all I can do is to review the matter and see that justice is done to the men, either by seeing that they get the full wages or by keeping back a certain amount from the contractor.

I am glad the minister has agreed to uphold the fair wage policy of the Dominion of Canada. The minister may have thought for a time that we on this side of the house were unreasonable, but I want to assure him that the stand we took was not because some $3,300 was at stake, but because the

I am glad the minister has agreed to see that these men will get a square deal, and I want to thank him for taking that position.

Then as soon as the government has pioneered and spent a large amount of money introducing these lines, when the population grows and a possible source of profit is developed, the British Columbia Telephone Company comes along and proposes to buy the line. While the service is still operating under a loss to the government the British Columbia Telephone Company buys the lines. The argument advanced by the government and to this house is, "Well, we were losing money; we had a chance to sell and we got rid of it." In several cases the fact has been demonstrated that while it might have been all right for the government to get rid of the lines, such a transfer was not in the best interests of the people concerned, because the telephone company took advantage of the situation to make such changes as they thought fit.
I shall now discuss another aspect of the situation. The government may say, what about our employees? In reply the British Columbia Telephone Company says with a wave of the hand, "we will take over your employees." They say, "we will certainly take care of your employees." "What about pension?" They may give a man what they wish; there is no agreement upon which he may depend. speechtext:
This is the amendment:
All the words including "provided" are struck out and replaced by the following:
Provided, however, that this subsection shall not apply to any private company, nor in case of any company whose shares, bonds, debentures or debenture stock are not offered for public subscription.

Mr. Chairman, I may say
that this bill was before the department of the Secretary of State, and I understand the Under-secretary of State appeared before the banking and commerce committee. In the opinion of the officers of the department there was no objection to this amendment if it applied only to private companies within the definition of the act, or to any other company which does not offer its bonds and shares for public subscription. The representations made to the department of state were to the effect that in many private companies the auditor was appointed by the shareholders and was also made a director. It was felt that in respect to private companies there should be no prohibition of an auditor being also one of the directors, because in his dual position he might be enabled the more efficiently to audit from day to day and week to week the affairs of the company.

Mr. Chairman, the Secretary
of State (Mr. Cahan) says that the practice of the auditor being also a director of the company is not objectionable provided it is restricted to a private company. But is there any particular reason why any auditor should be trusted to treat his relations
and friends in a different manner from that in which he would treat the general public? Let us suppose a case like this: Two men are in partnership, and perhaps their wives are included as shareholders in order to make the required number. One of the men acts as auditor. That is quite satisfactory as long as his partner is privy to the books and can at any time satisfy himself as to their cerrectness, but one of them dies. People do go wrong, and let us suppose that the remaining partner sets out to rob the other shareholders. He is allowed to continue as auditor, which was all right when his partner was alive, but after his partner dies he can do anything he likes and there is no protection to the widow or other private shareholders. If it is right in one case to protect the public it should be right, I think, to protect also the individuals who may happen to be shareholders in private companies. The woman, lacking business experience and knowing that her husband had confidence in his partner, might suppose it would be all right for him to continue. I know she could legally demand another auditor, but she would shrink from doing so because it would mean the breaking up of their friendship and of the partnership. I should like to hear the opinion of the Secretary of State in connection with a case of this kind.

I should think that was a very exceptional state of affairs. The number of shareholders in private companies is limited, and the shareholders not only elect the directors but have the duty and responsibility of appointing the auditor. I should think in that case if they wished to have an auditor-who must, I think, be a chartered accountant-and have the right to sit on the board of directors in order to watch the proceedings of the company, there is nothing in that dual situation which would be prejudicial to the interests of the shareholders as a whole. I do not think that case is likely to arise, where two partners form the company. There must be a certain number of shareholders anyway in a private company, not less than five and not more than fifty, I believe.
In British Columbia only three shareholders are required.

This is not the British
Columbia act; this is the dominion act. It has been represented to me also, Mr. Chairman, that a number of companies, of which the shareholders and the chief investors are resident in Great Britain, are operating in this

I think perhaps if the committee will assist the chairman a little more by reasonably observing the rule, the chairman will not find it necessary to bring members back more strictly to the rule, because once the chairman is called upon to rule, or does rule, he must rule according to the technical interpretation of the standing order.

When was the chairman
called upon to rule in connection with this discussion?

May I say to my hon.
friend in all kindness, and to two or three others to whom the observation may apply, that there has grown up recently a tendency to talk back at the chairman, which I think is very improper. The chairman makes a
Supply-Public Works

ruling; an hon. member has an opportunity to appeal against that ruling if it seems unfair or wrong. That is the proper procedure, but sometimes during a session of parliament hon. members get a little careless along certain lines. It is not necessarily the fault of any particular member; one follows another in, shall I say, a bad example or a course which is careless, and the house gets a little loose. That makes it very difficult for a chairman.
I am quite certain the chairman of committees is very efficient, I think we must compliment him upon his knowledge of the rules and his efficiency. I am sure if the house would cooperate with him a little more, and if these old practices were recognized and not abused, we would get along very much better and there would be more harmony and more expedition of the business of the house.
I find myself pretty much in accord with what the right hon. leader of the opposition has said. I might say one other word, however. Usually there are items of a general character, and quite often matters which are not strictly relevant to a particular item under discussion are left in abeyance until the general item is reached. For instance, there is dredging generally. Then when you come to public buildings, there are some large general items that permit of wide discussion. And under miscellaneous, there are items which warrant wider discussion. But I agree with the right hon. gentleman that if the minister in charge of the estimates, whatever the department may be, is willing to give the information-and generally speaking it has been the practice to allow discussion-the committee might depart somewhat from the strict interpretation of the rule.

I am not going to make any contrast between the practice followed this afternoon and the practice that has obtained in former years. I think the minister was very generous in answering all questions and giving all the information he had this afternoon, and I think he will agree with the leader of the opposition and with the last speaker, that time is saved by allowing a certain amount of latitude, so long as discussion is kept within reasonable bounds. I think the minister will agree that this has been the practice. Hon. members will recollect that, whenever public buildings, in Ontario or any other province, have been under consideration, in recent years at any rate, any hon. member who felt that some particular building had been unjustifiably omitted from the estimates has been allowed to point out the fact and to air his grievance. Of course, it seldom occurred under the late

administration that anyone had a justifiable grievance to air. But the practice has been to allow fairly wide latitude. I believe, Mr. Chairman, with great respect to yourself, that time would be saved if objection were not taken to everything that might not appear to be strictly within the rules.

In this quiet, friendly
atmosphere I wish to say something with which I think the whole committee will agree. My hon. friend and colleague will allow me to remind the committee and himself of one important matter which I have been bringing up in this house for many years. On many occasions I directed the attention of my hon. friend opposite, when he was minister, to the importance of the suggestion which I am about to renew, although I must confess I did so hopelessly. I refer to the question of the ventilation of this chamber. In common with many other hon. members now present, I have sat in this chamber for years-I have been here ever since the reconstruction of this building-and every summer I have had the same fault to find with the chamber. We swelter here simply because of the stubborn, I had almost said stupid, attitude of some engineers who have insisted upon leaving this chamber as it is. As I pointed out to the previous Minister of Public Works and to his predecessor as well, there are ways of making this chamber tolerable. At present it is not comfortable either in winter or in summer.
Nor sanitary.

Well, I am not going to
say that. But certainly it is not comfortable. It is too hot in summer, and it is also too hot in winter when the temperature could easily be regulated. I submit that this could be converted into a perfectly comfortable chamber. At the present time, however, there is not a room or a corridor in the whole building that is so hot. I urge now the importance of this matter, speaking not as Minister of Railways but as a doctor who in the old days knew something about sanitation and ventilation. This chamber is constructed pretty much on the principle of a cathedral, and if the upper windows were opened we might get some fresh air. I know the present minister is a gentleman of an intelligent and conciliatory type, and I have no doubt he will get his officers to do something about it. I suggest that the upper windows be opened so as to permit the hot air to escape-and I hasten to add that I am not for a moment making any rude insinuation with regard to any of the speeches

Supply-Public Works
delivered here. I am merely suggesting that we allow the warm air, such as naturally rises in any building in which there is a congregation or an assembly, to escape, so that we might be saved the torture of a sort of Turkish bath in the chamber. I do not want to delay my colleague's estimates, but I do suggest, in all earnestness, that something be done to make the chamber comfortable. It is anything but comfortable at any time. Frankly, we have not had a ventilation system in this chamber worth a hoot.

I would suggest that it
might be wise for the minister to examine the ventilation system in the grill room of the Chateau Laurier. There is no better ventilation in the dominion than there is in that grill room.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I wish to thank hon.
members for their remarks and to assure them that, if I appear to apply the rules rigidly, I am merely trying my best to do my duty. I shall be grateful for any suggestions from the committee, but I am bound by standing order 58. However, when it is evident that there is no objection on the part of the committee, I allow the widest latitude.

In the spirit
in which you have received the remarks of the committee, Mr. Chairman, may I submit that if you will give a broad interpretation to the word "item" we shall meet what I believe to be the desire of the committee generally. Section 2 of standing order 58 reads:
Speeches in committee of the whole house must be strictly relevant to the item or clause under consideration.
We are now on item 210, which is under the heading "miscellaneous." If the opposition wished to take up time, they might ask that every one of the different sub-items under the head of "miscellaneous" be called and voted upon separately. We might be prepared, however, having looked over the estimate, to vote item 210 as a whole, if there were a broad interpretation of the term " miscellaneous," which would afford hon. members an opportunity of discussing such matters as they have not been able so far to take up. We are now on "public works- chargeable to income," and if we could take up these various matters by provinces there would be little difficulty in the way of violation of the rule on account of the discussion being carried too far. With this general understanding I believe we ought to make better headway.
In connection with the item, "national monument on Connaught place," what expenditures were made last year?

The original
amount of the contract was 8135,000, and that was added to for two additional figures costing $10,000. This makes a total of $145,000. There has been paid on this contract, to March 31, 1931, the sum of $94,500, so that the amount to complete the contract in 1931-32 is $50,500-say $50,000.
If there is a contract, I suppose we must go through with it. But with poor unemployed soldiers in the country, I do not think we shall need many monuments for a while.

The contract
was entered into some years ago under circumstances which I think thoroughly warranted it. The monument will be very creditable to the country, and when the work is complete, and these hard times are past,
I think my hon. friend will approve of it.
Under the item "authorized by statute", are those the usual amounts voted?
Those are subsidies.

Before this item passes, I
should like to discuss a little matter with the Minister of Public Works, under the item: "Engineering branch-salaries of engineers".
I would ask the indulgence of the committee because it may appear that I am straying from the subject. I would have brought this matter to the attention of the minister much sooner, but I had not the information that I now have. It may seem that I shall be stretching the point a little, but I am keeping in mind the engineering branch and around that I shall try to centre my remarks.
On June 1, I put some questions on the order paper as follows:
1.	Have any of the contracts which were let last year in connection with the protection work on the Fraser river been subsequently sublet by the original contractors?
2.	If so, what are the names of the subcontractors and what portion or portions of the contract work have been sublet?
3.	Was permission granted to the said contractors before any of the work was sublet?
4.	If so, by whom was permission granted, and what was the date of such authorization?
5.	What are the names of the contractors who have sublet any of the original contracts?
The answer which the Minister of Public Works gave to that was:
No information.
Supply-Public Works

I believe I have considerable information and I should like to lay it before him because I consider it to be of a very serious nature. In fact, before I have finished my remarks I shall ask that an inquiry be held into the whole matter, so grave are the charges made in regard to some of the work being done on the Fraser river.
On September 30, 1930, a contract was let on the Fraser river for some $350,000 to the Jaynes Construction Company for work on the south jetty, Fraser river, at Steveston. They started out using a high line to place the rock there. That system failed. They subsequently sublet the work to the Kennedy Construction Company. According to the minister's reply to my question, he has no information that that work had been sublet. The information I have is that the Jaynes Construction Company is off the job entirely and that the subcontractors have undertaken it. They tried to do the work with a steam shovel, and the steam shovel failed. They then employed men, and the information which I have under my hand is that hand work was very necessary in the placing of this heavy rock. Trouble arose regarding the subcontractors having obtained this contract at a low price, figuring they could use a steam shovel and would not be compelled to employ men, but they were forced to employ men owing to the strict supervision of the work, and they also attempted to beat the men, if I may use that expression, out of some of their money. Mr. Harrison of the Labour department was called out there in an endeavour to settle this dispute. Some correction may probably be necessary before I am through, and, if so, I would be glad if the minister would make it. But the information that I have is that word was sent to Ottawa recommending that these men be paid one hour extra from September 30, 1930, up to the spring of this year. They have been paid only from January 12 or a period of three months, and they still lack three months' back pay. This subcontractor and the Jaynes Construction Company are the only companies that have tried to diverge from established practice on the river: that is, when men have to be taken out to the work and have to wait on rock coming, they are paid a certain amount for time going back and forth and waiting on the rock arriving. That has been the practice that has been followed by nearly all companies with the exception of these two.
I understand now that the shovel is again being put into use and that the men have been laid off. This is serious enough during 
these times, but the recommendation of the engineer or superintendent in charge was that this work could be done far better and the rock placed to better advantage by hand, the rock being what is termed "one-man size rock". The subcontractor, however, has taken the contract from the original contractor at such a low price that, unless he uses a steam shovel, he is not going to break even or make any money, and so he wants to use a steam shovel in preference to the men.
I have three complaints. The first is that the contractor had no right to sublet the contract without the minister's knowledge or sanction, because so much money is involved and the work is of such importance. I am informed that the original contractors have not appeared on the job since the work was sublet. My complaint is that the contract should not have been allowed to be sublet without the minister's permission. My second complaint is that these men ought to receive the extra back pay from September, 1930. My third complaint is this: that the subcontractor took the job at too low a figure is no reason why the steam shovel should be allowed to operate, and besides, the work can be done to better advantage by hand. That was the recommendation of the superintendent in charge, and the information I have, whether it be right or wrong, is that that recommendation was also sent by the district engineer to the department some time during this spring.
These are three charges, and I think they are serious enough to warrant an inquiry. This is a large contract. Not only are the rights of the men involved, but the work is so important to the Fraser river that I think the whole scheme should be looked into with a view of seeing what is going on there. The minister says that he has no information in connection with this matter. I may tell him I have been besieged with letters and telegrams. Only to-day I received a telegram from the council who are up in arms in regard to the matter, and they say they are sending me a file containing information. I have a good deal of correspondence from others and from the men concerned, and I would ask the minister to have an inquiry made into the whole matter, namely, the subcontract, the men's wages, and the question of the steam shovel.

The allegations
of my hon. friend are serious enough to warrant an investigation and careful consideration. We have not been asked to sanction any assignment of the contract, and therefore

Supply-Public Works
the matter has not been brought to our attention, neither has my hon. friend until this time brought to my attention the information which he has on his file.
I got it only this morning.

Otherwise I
might have been able to investigate the matter and give him more information. I want, however, to assure him that the chief engineer is very much interested in the work on the Fraser river; he realizes the importance of it; he has made a special study of conditions there, and we are following up very closely what has been done, with a view to securing the best result. I am not sure that we can dictate to a contractor whether he shall employ men or machinery so long as he does the work properly within the specifications and to the satisfaction of our engineer. Desirable though it might be, from the standpoint of relieving unemployment, to have the work done by hand instead of by machinery, so long as the work is properly done we have no control over the means employed, because probably the work can be done by the contractor more cheaply by machinery than by hand. But all these matters will be referred to the chief engineer who will check and follow them up, and if there are any conditions that require remedying, they will be attended to.

When was the contract
let?
September, 1930.

Has the minister any information whether the district engineer at any time since the work started recommended that men be used instead of the steam shovel? These' allegations have been made to me in perfectly good faith and I should like to know whether they are correct or not. The allegation that has been made to me is that the district engineer at some time between September and the present time recommended that the use of the steam shovel be discontinued.

I understand from the chief engineer that some representations were made in connection with the steam shovel, that it was discontinued, and that a strike followed. I do not know what happened after that. May I say that if my hon. friend has information of this kind coming to him from time to time and will come to the office, he will get the information he requires more readily and more completely than I am able to give it here on the spur of the moment.

I realize that, and in fairness let me say that I should have been only too pleased to come to the office had I had the information earlier, but I had to send back for it and it reached me only very recently. Another point that I should like cleared up is with regard to the men's wages. Has any recommendation been made by the Department of Labour that the men's wages be made retroactive to September, 1930?
I have no information on that subject. It is a matter for the Department of Labour.
I am informed that the first report of the Minister of Labour was that the men's wages be made retroactive to September of last year and up until the strike took place.
I can assure my hon. friend that any recommendations from the Department of Labour that are calculated to do justice to the men will be enforced by the Public Works department.
May I have the assurance from the minister that a full inquiry will be made regarding this sub-contract and how the work is being carried out, and that the question of wages will also be looked into?
I shall ask the chief engineer to make inquiries and see what should be done.

We had a very full discussion this afternoon with respect to the fair wage and the eight hour day clauses pertaining to public contracts, after which the minister very rightly acceded to the representations made and promised that the men would receive their back pay in accordance with that particular contract. As I left the chamber, a representative of these labour men who was sitting in the gallery told me that he had knowledge of the fact that the contractor had intimated to the men that if they insisted upon urging that their rightful wages be paid they would be discriminated against, that any of them not now working would not be reemployed, and that any of them working would be dismissed. The point I want to make, and I am sure the committee will agree with me, is this, that it is about time the parliament of Canada put its stamp of disapproval upon any contractor doing business with the government of Canada who would undertake in any way, shape or form to intimidate the men on his job because they insist upon their rights. I draw this to the attention of the minister at this time because I think if there is no other recourse the

Supply-Public Works
minister and the government would be perfectly in order in advising any contractor who would take such high-handed action that no more public contracts would be granted to him.
I can assure my hon. friend that we have no sympathy with any practices of that sort. I am not aware that anything of that kind has occurred.

In the spring of 1929.,
in the Porcupine district, between South Porcupine and Golden City, there was quite a flood on the Porcupine river. In conjunction with the provincial government officers some of the federal engineers made inquiry into the situation and some thousands of dollars was spent in 1929 to remedy the situation, which had caused quite a lot of damage to some of the people along that stream. I believe that the engineering branch of the Department of Public Works in the month of June sent a report to the department recommending that $700 be spent for the purpose of removing some large boulders from the first rapids of the Porcupine river. Luckily we had no floods this spring, but a flood situation may recur in the fall or later. For reasons absolutely unknown to me and to the people of that district, not a cent of that proposed expenditure of $700 was spent last year. I trust that the department will find it possible this year to remove those boulders which are really a menace, I will not say to navigation, but in regard to causing floods such as we have had in the past. I hope that the minister will receive these representations in the same spirit in which I make them. In 1930 when money was spent in that section of the country nobody could complain that there was any political interference with that expenditure. Very little public money has ever been spent in northern Ontario. I believe that this expenditure which I am now urging should be made at this time of the year, because later in the fall we may have to face a flood situation which we are not likely to have in the height of the summer.

I will take the
suggestions of my hon. friend into consideration, and if circumstances will permit and funds warrant, we will see what can be done to relieve the situation.

The funds were available last year, but I do not believe there is any need of any special fund. This is an urgent work and it would be possible for the department to go ahead and do it this year. It is only a small item, but it is very im-
portant to that section of the country. If you will look over the estimates you will find that not a single dollar is being spent for public works in my riding or in the riding of my hon. friend the Minister of Immigration.

If I am correctly informed, there was no specific appropriation for this work last year. The cost would have to be borne out of the general vote. As to my hon. friend's complaint that no money is being expended in his constituency and in others, a good many of my friends here are making the same complaint this year, and have done so in years gone by. I think my hon. friend has had a public building recently.

That is no answer to
my question. Surely the minister does not insinuate that because a small town of 14,000 people has got a public building, we are getting more than our share.
The hon. gentleman said that no public money had been spent in his constituency.

The information I
gathered last year was that this expenditure I am urging could be made out of the appropriation for dredging. I want to be fair, as I know the minister does. I understand that he is trying to curtail expenditure in his department, but the fact remains that there is a menace of a flood situation in that section which could easily be removed by the expenditure of a very small sum of money.
I hope, therefore, that the government will find it possible to make the expenditure this year.
I have requested the chief engineer to look into it and see if provision can be made for it, and if possible it will be taken care of.

With reference to the item of $100,000 for the national gallery of Canada, last year I tried to persuade the then Minister of Public Works to provide more facilities for the. public to visit the gallery and museum, but I do not think I was very successful in my efforts. I understand that the present hours at which the gallery and museum are open to the public are from nine or ten in the morning until six in the evening.
I do not know whether that statement is correct, but it is not veiy far out. The whole purpose for which a gallery and museum are erected and maintained is lost when we do not give the general public an opportunity to

Supply-Public Works
visit the building. I have been there once or twice during the hours of the day, and with the exception of the policemen on duty there was hardly a soul in the whole building. I think we should follow the practice of opening the building a little later in the morning, and keeping it open until, say, nine at night, in order to give the great body of our citizens and visitors to the city the opportunity to inspect the works of art and other exhibits; for the public should get something out of the vast amount of money that has been spent on the very valuable collection at the museum. Better facilities should be afforded to the general public for visiting the building, and I can think of no good reason why it should not be kept open four or five nights a week until about nine o'clock, with the exception of the summer months. During the winter occasional social functions are held at night, when a limited number of people are allowed to inspect the recent additions to the art treasures. Although I agree that these occasional social functions during the winter are desirable, it would also be a good thing to have the building open for inspection on winter evenings for the benefit of the general public.
Further, I should like to see the exhibits in the national museum utilized to a greater extent than they are at the present time, and to that end, I think the department should consider the advisability of arranging a travelling exhibit so that the people in the towns and cities other than Ottawa, or areas where there are facilities for exhibition, may have an opportunity of seeing at least many of the works of art housed in the national gallery. It should not involve a large expenditure to do this, and I am quite sure other cities and towns in the dominion would be only too pleased to undertake the care of these treasures. I suggest that they be sent from Halifax right through to Victoria. I have no doubt that such action would be deeply appreciated by the people in all parts of the dominion.
I make only those two suggestions: First, that greater facilities should be given to the people of Ottawa to visit the institution, and secondly, that serious consideration be given to the question of a travelling exhibit of treasures of the art gallery.

I agree with the hon. member that the measure of value of the art gallery is the extent to which it is made accessible to and used by the public. My hon. friend undoubtedly knows that the gallery is administered by a board of trustees who carefully consider the policies and programs best
calculated to make the gallery available to the Canadian public. I understand that from time to time the trustees have made loan exhibits along the lines mentioned by my hon. friend.
Concerning the visiting hours, I have some information before me. The national gallery exhibition halls are open to the public every week day in the year from 10 a.m. to 5 p,m., all holidays included with the exception of Christmas day. On Sundays the gallery is open in the afternoons from 2 o'clock until 5 o'clock. The experiment of keeping the institution open in the evenings until 10 p.m., except in the summer months, is being tried. Thus far the evening attendance has never exceeded 10 per cent of the day attendance, but the intention is to continue the experiment next autumn. I have received this information from the trustees.
May I say that the trustees will be informed of the suggestions by my hon. friend, and I am sure they will welcome any worth while suggestions and adopt any programs that appear to be calculated to make the operation of the gallery more effective and more accessible to the public.

If the experiment of keeping the gallery open until 10 p.m. is being tried I think it should be made known. I do not think the general public is aware that that is being done. Probably it was not patronized because there was no public notice of the hours when visiting would be allowed. I should be pleased if the minister would place before the proper authorities the question of loan exhibits to the municipalities in the various parts of the dominion.
I will see that the trustees are made aware of my hon. friend's suggestions.
Can the minister give the committee any information as to the number of temporary employees in the Department of Public Works?
I would suggest to my hon. friend that we might discuss that matter when the items of civil government are under consideration.
Coming back to the national gallery, may I ask how the 8100,000 was spent?

This amount of 8100,000 was requested by the board of trustees to provide for the operation and maintenance of workshops, supplies, upkeep of premises, purchase of works of art, management expenses, and the usua' travelling
Supply-Public Works

scholarship of the National Gallery of Canada for the fiscal year 1931-32. If my hon. friend wishes, I shall enumerate the different items of expenditure for the year 1930-31. The works of art purchased were valued at $105,560; salaries, $7,040; general maintenance, including exhibition work in Canada and reproduction of pictures for schools, $17,400, making a total for that year of $130,000.
Item agreed to.

I would ask
that the committee now revert to item 194 of the estimates.
Harbours and rivers-Prince Edward Island, $50,500.

When this item was discussed on a previous occasion the minister was good enough to allow it to stand, with the promise that he would bring down certain information. The information is now before us, and I think it bears out fully the contention we made at that time, namely, that the contract in question had actually been given to a gentleman who had never submitted a tender. In this connection I do not wish to deal harshly with the minister, because the unfortunate circumstance is no fault of his. I think however the fault is that of his good friend down in Summerside, Prince Edward Island, who advised him in this matter and requested that instead of the contract being left with Mr. Maynard, the tenderer to whom it was transferred by Mr. Campbell, it be given to a man who had not submitted a tender. Possibly it is all right to give Mr. Downing the contract, but I would ask the minister to remember that there are other pebbles on the beach down in Prince Edward Island besides Mr. Downing. There were a-number of good Conservative contractors who would have welcomed a chance to tender for this work. If my good friend the minister could not see his way clear to give the contract to one of the legal tenderers, I think in all fairness to the public, and also to his own department and to lift it above suspicion, he should have called for new tenders. If he found it impossible to allow a legal tenderer to get the contract just because he happened to be a Liberal, I think in justice to the other Conservative contractors in the province he should have called for new tenders. These papers were brought down on May 5th. I find there is a letter dated April 2nd from the department to Mr. * Downing requesting him to sign a contract, but up to that time he had not done so, and there is nothing on the file produced to show that he ever did sign a contract.

I would point out that his vote was chargeable to the supplementary estimates of 1930, and my contention is that as these estimates lapsed on the 31st of March, 1930, the public works department could not enter into a contract with Mr. Downing in April of this year. I believe that as yet no contract has been entered into with Mr. Downing. Indeed I should be surprised to learn that they did enter into a contract after the 31st day of March, when, as I say, these estimates lapsed. Mr. Campbell was notified that 'the only way in which he could avoid forfeiting his deposit cheque was to have someone take over the contract. By the way, I have heard it stated in the corridors of this building, and I have seen it reported in the newspapers in Prince Edward Island, that I had requested that the contract be transferred to Mr. Maynard. I can assure my hon. friends opposite that they can find no telegram or letter from me making any such suggestion. All I did was to telegraph the department to return Mr. Campbell his cheque after the contract had been transferred to Mr. Maynard by the department. This is the telegram of August 5, 1930, from the Deputy Minister of Public Works to myself :
Department can allow Campbell to withdraw tender railway wharf, Summerside, only provided deposit is forfeited or whatever portion thereof necessary to make up amount of next lowest tender, which is $7,472.50 if second tenderer now willing to take contract at price of his bid.
The second tenderer, Mr. Maynard, did take the contract at the price of Mr. Campbell's bid, and sent his deposit cheque. That cheque was received by the department and sent over to the finance department on August 21 Mr. Campbell was certainly bound to the department when he put up his deposit cheque. That being so, the department in turn was bound to Mr. Campbell. All that happened was this: Air. Campbell withdrew, Mr. Maynard stepped into Mr. Campbell's shoes and put up the deposit cheque as requested by the department. Then he became bound to the department, and in turn the department became bound to him. I think this is proved by the following letter of August 21, 1930, which was sent by the chief accountant of the public works department to the Deputy Minister of Finance:
On 31st July last, amongst other security cheques transmitted to your department, there was one amounting to $738, given by Mr. J. E. Campbell, as security for a contract for the reconstruction of the railway wharf at Summer-side, Prince Edward Island. Since that date, for good and sufficient reasons-

Supply-Public Works
I wish the minister would listen to these
words:
Since that date, for good and sufficient reasons, it has been decided that Mr. Campbell should be permitted to transfer his contract in this matter to Mr. W. R. Maynard. Mr. Maynard has now put up a security deposit for the same amount, which is enclosed herein.
If there is anything which closes a bargain between man and man certainly that conclusively closed the deal with Mr. Maynard. The accountant requested the Deputy Minister of Einance to return Mr. Campbell's cheque. That cheque was thereupon returned to the accountant and forwarded by him to Mr. Campbell. Later on this matter was referred to council. I do not think that full information was given 'to council at the time, otherwise I do not believe they would have acted as they did. Apparently before this the matter had been referred to the solicitor of the department, because they wished to be sure they were preceding within the four corners of the a.ct. The departmental solicitor gave his opinion in this letter of September 4, 1930:
In connection with this I would draw your attention to the clause in the tender reading as follows:
The security cheque or bonds will be forfeited if the person or persons tendering refuse to enter into a contract when called upon to do so.
Then he continues:
As contractual relationship is established by offer and acceptance, I submit that in this case Mr. Campbell was bound by his offer as represented by his tender and that from that time the Crown had option of,
(a)	Insisting upon the specific performance of the contract, or
(b)	Holding Mr. Campbell's security deposit and arranging for a new contract.
What they did was to allow Mr. Campbell to arrange wiith the second tenderer. That is also pointed out in this telegram sent to Mr. J. F. Arnett by the minister himself on September 4:
Re building portion railway wharf Summer-side. Campbell arranged with next lowest tenderer W. R. Maynard, Northam, Prince Edward Island, to take over his contract at Campbell's price, namely $7,380. Maynard sent cheque for deposit required, namely $738. and Campbell's cheque was returned. If H. M. Downing whom you sugest -will forward marked cheque for $738 department will recommend contract be made with him.
Now, in fairness to everyone concerned in this matter, I would have no objection in the world to Mr. Downing getting the contract if he had been a regular tenderer. But I submit, Mr. Chairman, that it was absolutely unfair for the department to go outside of the four regular tenderers and give the contract to a man who never had tendered. I appeal to the minister in order that he may lift his department above suspicion and put the country at rest regarding the matter, that if he cannot see his way clear to award the contract to W. R. Maynard-to whom in all fairness it should be awarded-then the least he can do is to call for new tenders.
Has the work been started?

My information is that
the work has not been started. I know the minister will state that Mr. Campbell offered to transfer this contract to Mr. Downing. I wired Mr. Campbell when this matter was up previously, asking if he ever offered to transfer this contract to Mr. Downing. He replied:
Do not remember suggesting Downing to take over contract. How could I when I did not have the arranging of same?
That proves conclusively that Campbell never offered to transfer the contract to Downing; Campbell was completely out of the picture previous to that date and Maynard had taken over the contract at Campbell's figures. He had forwarded his deposit cheque to the department; it had been accepted and forwarded to the Department of Finance. The Department of Public Works returned Campbell's cheque and released him from all obligations, and my contention is that if Campbell -was bound, Maynard was also bound; if Campbell or Maynard were bound to the department, then in all fairness as between man and man the department also were bound to Campbell or Maynard. They admit that they were bound to Campbell, and they were a party to the transfer of the contract to Maynard, so I think Maynard was equally bound.
This matter was referred to council on September 4, but I do not believe the department gave full information to council in connection with the transfer of the contract from Campbell to Maynard. I find no mention in this order in council of Mr. Maynard. An order in council was passed on August 5, 1930, accepting the lowest tender. Mr. Campbell was notified of the acceptance of his tender, and he subsequently advised the department that he wished to be relieved. Apparently that was the information given to council by the department. I have not a copy of the letter written by the department to council asking that this order in council be passed, but I think if they had stated that Mr. Maynard had taken over the contract from Mr. Campbell, council would not have passed this order in council awarding the contract to Mr. Downing.
Supply-Public Works

I do not know whether or not I have made myself clear, but all I ask at the present time, in all fairness, is that the minister advertise for new tenders. He should give the contract to Mr. Maynard; there is absolutely no reason in the world why that should not be done. Mr. Maynard deposited his cheque in good faith, as he was requested to do by the department. Mr. Downing never submitted a tender, and it is absolutely unfair and completely destroys the tender system of this country if the Department of Public Works or any other department of government, after getting the lowest of a number of tenders, is to go outside and ask for private bids from people who never tendered at all.
In conclusion I should like first to point out that contracts for over $5,000 must be let by public tender. In this case that was not done; the minister himself acknowledges that Mr. Downing never submitted a tender. In the second place the lowest tender must be accepted. In this case, after the lowest tender was accepted, it was used by the department to get a bid from an outsider who did not tender. In the third place, this money was voted in the supplementary estimates of 1930. Those estimates had lapsed, and I submit the department could not legally enter into a contract in connection with which the money voted had lapsed. A contract cannot be entered into legally until the money is voted or revoted. This money has not been revoted, and the contract was not signed on May 5, when these papers were brought down. In addition, when the case was referred to council, as I.say the facts were not all given. It was not mentioned that Campbell had transferred his tender to Mr. Maynard. I also submit that Mr. Downing never submitted a contract and that when Maynard asked the department to send back his deposit cheque they held it until February of this year, when they wrote and stated it was an oversight that the cheque had not been returned sooner.
It is my contention that an agreement was entered into between Mr. Maynard and the department which should be carried out, and I say the department had no right to enter into a contract with Downing. Maynard was a bona fide tenderer; he fulfilled his part of the obligation and did everything the department asked him to do. I do not think any hon. member of this house will rise in his place and say Maj'nard was treated fairly. All I am asking is a fair deal, and I trust the minister will give it.

In reference
to what the hon. member for Prince has been

stating, my attention has been directed to representations which appeared in the press of Prince Edward Island in reference to my remarks the other evening in connection with this matter. Apparently the inference was drawn that in some way I was reflecting upon the hon. member for Prince when I said I thought an unnecessary amount of time had been taken up in discussing the item. I think the text of my remarks will show that my criticism was directed against the minister. All that was being asked for was the production of papers, and I could not understand why an hour should be taken up in deciding whether or not those papers should be brought down. I just want to make that point clear.
Carried.

No, it is not carried; I
want some information from the minister first. Would the minister tell the committee when the contract was sent to Mr. Downing to be signed?
October 8, 1930.

Did he sign the contract
and return it?

The contract
has been signed and returned.
When?

I do not know
exactly, but we have the signed contract. It is not unusual for a contractor to delay in returning his duplicate of the contract.

But it is unusual for a
contractor to delay five months in returning the contract. On March 20, 1931, this contractor had not returned the signed contract. Further, I am informed that it had not been returned by April 2. In spite of that, the department gave him an extension of. time in which to complete the work. The date for the completion of this work was extended to February 1, 1931, yet that contractor had not signed his contract though it had been in his possession for three or four months.
I cannot say on what date he signed it; all I can say is he had not returned it. It might have been signed months before.

On December 26 Downing
was notified by your department that he had not signed this contract, and he was asked as to the cause of the delay. On March 20, 1931, the department wrote him again, but he did not reply. In the meanwhile, the time for the completion of that work was extended,

Business of the House
without knowledge on the part of the department that the contract had been signed. They had no contract and therefore they had no right to extend the time for the completion of the work.
I assumed that the contract had been signed but that the formality of returning it had not been complied with.
Neither the department nor the district engineer had been notified that it was signed.
Carried.
You will get it carried all the sooner if you keep quiet. Will the minister tell me when that contract, signed, was received in the office?
Recently, within the last month or so.

Then, when it lapsed on March 31, the department did not know that the contract had been accepted. The amount lapsed on March 31. How can the minister, before even this amount is voted, carry on under that contract, the amount for which had lapsed? The contract was not signed in time to make use of the money voted in 1930.
My hon. friend has no right to say that the contract was not signed in time.

I say that the contract, so far as the department is concerned, is not signed until the department knows that the signature is appended to it, and the contract is received and recorded in the department. Otherwise, the department cannot act upon it. The department prepared their estimates in the month of February. How could they put in a revote when they did not 'have a signed contract in the department and had no knowledge that the contract was signed, except the supposition that it had been signed and was being held by the contractor? There was no contract in the department. The minister prepared his estimates, with the revote, in the month of February. The old vote " lapsed on March 31. On that date he had nothing in the department to show that this man had signed the contract, and he did not get it until a few days ago. Yet he comes to the committee and asks us to vote this amount of money to be paid over to a contractor who has not a contract legally.
Mr. MaciLEAN: Never tendered.

But even if he had tendered, the offer he made ends; it has gone by. It is no good, and therefore the minister will be perfectly justified in calling for new tenders. That is why I raised the point. He would be justified in calling for new tenders, and the department should do so.
The hon. gentleman will realize on reflection that if the contract was not signed and the contractor did not do the work, the money will not be paid to him. That is all.
That is only a red herring.

I wish to say a word now in reply to my hon. friend from Prince (Mr. MacLean). The bon. gentleman will recall that this lowest tenderer was anxious to be relieved of the contract, and on August 28, when Mr. Arnett communicated with the Department of Public Works, he stated in his communication that Mr. Campbell would assign the contract if necessary. He had been in touch with Mr. Downing and was prepared to assign the contract to him. He did not care to get the contract so long as he was relieved.
The minister is absolutely wrong, becausp I have read the telegram, in which Campbell denies that he had any conference with Arnett or Downing.

The telegram is
here, and the only inference from it is that Campbell had communicated with Downing.

And I say that Campbell personally denied it asbsolutely.
Progress reported.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in moving the adjournment of the house I desire to intimate that we shall take the estimates of .the Interior department and those of National Defence on Monday, followed by Public Works-that is, if we get into supply.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
We all realize,
of course, that the Prime Minister must arrange the business as he thinks desirable. I hope, however, that he will not too long delay consideration of the ways and means resolutions. At the special session, as my right hon. friend remembers, matters were rushed through rapidly, and it would be helpful at this session to bring on the resolutions fairly early.
Business oj the House

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
As there are two or
three departments which have not yet been m supply, the purpose of proceeding on Monday is to get them into supply. I will expedite as far as possible the bringing in of the resolutions, but I desire to see that every department has been in supply so that we may call them whenever there is an opportunity.
I can say that there will be no disposition to embarrass the Prime Minister in regard to any departments he wishes to take up.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That will help.

My right hon friend will remember, however, that I asked him whether we might have at an early date comparative tables of the various items in the tariff changes proposed and that he promised he would see that something of the kind was prepared.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I propose to make available to every member of the house an office consolidation of a copy of the customs tariff. When I last inquired, the comparative table was being prepared of the changes made this year in last year's tariff.

Will they be
available?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am hoping they will
be available the first of the week. To-morrow will settle all that so far as I am concerned. I have not had time to deal with matters of that kind in the last few davs.

Monday will
be devoted to estimates entirely?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That was what I was
hoping to do-to get into supply those departments which have not yet been in, so that there might be no delay in taking advantage of any opportunity to call them.
Motion agreed to and the house adjourned at 10.58 p.m.
Monday, June 22, 1931.
